prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, which opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: In my opening ballot I placed IceCube (B013) first because it is the discovery I can judge most closely as an experimentalist. Having read all eight ballots, I now think the committee's best-supported and most defensible prize is the magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene candidate (B022). It is the only shortlisted candidate that seven of eight members rank in their top three and that all eight rank at all, and three members place it first. The case is intrinsically strong: a 2011 theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic angle (Bistritzer and MacDonald) followed by the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators), a classic prediction-then-observation sequence that created an entire field, replicated across many laboratories and platforms. All eight members proposed the same three names, so the supplied attribution is the least contested on the shortlist. A theory-plus-experiment configuration of three people also fits the statutes without strain, and the observed phenomena were measured in nature rather than inferred from models.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old, the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder complicates some phases, so a citation must be worded around the prediction and the observation rather than any microscopic explanation. The experimental credit is also wider than one group: Cory Dean's hBN-based devices, and the Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani groups made major contributions that are not in the supplied names, and a three-person cap forces an uncomfortable cut. Recognition now could look early next to the more mature optical lattice clocks (B012), whose 10^-18 performance has been confirmed by several laboratories and whose practical impact is near.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B022 first as a field-defining theory-plus-experiment story, but warns that the experimental credit extends beyond the single listed experimentalist and that the interpretation of the superconductivity is still evolving.
responses.response: I accept both qualifications and they are why I would keep the citation narrow: prediction of the magic angle and discovery of the correlated and superconducting states, with no claim about pairing mechanism. I do not think the credit gap, which exists for nearly every candidate here, is large enough to disqualify the pairing of Bistritzer-MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero's 2018 observations. I would, however, want the committee to examine the author record of the first reports before final votes, since Dean's group is the most serious omission.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B012) first because the progress is set by measurement accuracy, the Katori-Ye attribution is clean and the independent confirmation at 10^-18 is established.
responses.response: I agree with him on attribution and maturity: B012 has the cleanest two-name credit on the list and I ranked it fourth for that reason. Where I differ is that B022 carries wider breadth of impact and much broader cross-member support, while B012 won only three first places and was ranked in the top three by only four members. I regard B012 as the strongest alternative and would support it if the committee judges that the moire field is still too young; I would not accept the argument that the 2005 comb prize makes it redundant.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator candidate (B018) second and describes it as timely and arguably overdue, while noting that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I ranked B018 second myself and share his view of its importance, but the omission of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction is, for me, a real defect in any three-name prize, because the experiment by Molenkamp's group was directly motivated by it, and the 2016 prize on topological phases overlaps in theme. That is why I now place it behind B022, whose theory-experiment pairing is not undermined by a comparable missing name. I would not rule B018 out if the committee can agree a citation that avoids implying priority for the HgTe prediction.

responses.point: Johansson ranks quantum key distribution (B038) first and quantum error correction (B025) fifth, but puts B022 only sixth, calling it slightly premature given the unresolved superconductivity mechanism and twist-angle disorder.
responses.response: I take the prematurity point seriously, and I treat it as the main reason this is not a unanimous choice. My answer is that the prize recognises a prediction and an observation that have been reproduced independently, not an explanation of the pairing mechanism, and the discovery of tunable correlated and superconducting phases is already secure. For B038 I note that only two members ranked it at all, and the Ekert spelling duplicate in the credited names would have to be resolved, so I cannot see a route to broad support there at this stage.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied experimental credit is sufficient, in particular the role of Cory Dean's group and of the first author of the 2018 papers relative to Jarillo-Herrero.
Whether the committee regards eight years as enough maturity for the moire field, and how much weight the unsettled superconducting mechanism should carry in the citation wording.

Whether a two-part prize combining one moire name with B012 would be preferable to a single three-person B022 prize; I have not found a split that is fair to both sets of credited names within the three-person limit.
The IceCube credit (Halzen, Spiering) omits AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers, and source identification remains partial, which is why I no longer put B013 first despite my own opening ranking.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records membership in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and a field-adjacent background in astroparticle detection, which touches B013 (IceCube) and, more loosely, B027 and B008 as instrumentation cases; no documented tie to the credited individuals of those candidates is recorded, so it is a matter of field proximity rather than a recusal issue. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B022, the preferred configuration.
